title: Your right to remain silent
summary: When you are arrested, you do not have to answer questions. You cannot be forced to say anything that could be used against you.
body_plain: The Constitution says a person who is arrested or detained has the right to remain silent or to avoid answering any question until they have consulted a lawyer or a person of their own choice. In addition, no one charged with an offence can be compelled to give evidence against themselves at trial. Staying silent is not an admission of guilt - it is a protected right.
rights: You may remain silent until you speak to a lawyer (s.35(2)).
You cannot be compelled to give evidence against yourself (s.36(11)).
Silence is not an admission of guilt.
do_list: Say clearly: 'I wish to remain silent until I speak to my lawyer.'
Give only your basic identity if required, then wait for your lawyer.
Note anyone who pressures you to talk.
dont_list: Do not feel forced to explain or defend yourself on the spot.
Do not let anyone tell you that staying silent proves guilt.
common_situations: Police ask detailed questions about an allegation before you have legal advice.
You are told that silence proves guilt or will automatically prevent bail.
An officer asks you to write, record, correct, or sign a statement.
words_to_use: I wish to remain silent until I have consulted my lawyer or another person of my choice.
Please record that I am exercising my constitutional right to remain silent.
I will provide my basic identifying information, but I will not answer questions about the allegation without advice.
if_violated: Remember who questioned you, when you requested silence or legal advice, and whether questioning continued.
Tell your lawyer about threats, promises, force, recording, or any statement you made or signed.
Preserve copies of statements, interview records, messages, or witness details.

citations.source_name: 1999 Constitution of the Federal Republic of Nigeria
